transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You found the friction force correctly. Can you check if the normal force is really 49 N on an incline?
Um, isn't normal force just the weight? 5 times 9.8 is 49. I don't get what's wrong.
Okay, let me think.
On an incline, the normal force is not the same as the weight. It's less than the weight because the surface is tilted.
I don't understand. Why would tilting it make it less? How much less?
Good question. One moment.
Good question. On an incline, only part of the weight pushes straight into the surface, so the normal force is less than the full weight.
Okay but I don't know how to work out that part. What do I actually do?
Let me see.
You're on the right track with the formula, but the normal force isn't 49 N on an incline. Try breaking the weight into components.
Components? I don't know what that means. Can you just show me?
Got it. Give me a second.
Components mean breaking the weight into parts. The part pushing straight into the incline is the normal force. We'll find that next.
Okay, so how do I find it?
Okay, let me think.
To find the friction force, first find the normal force using the weight and the angle.
Using the angle how? Like 49 times 30? I really don't get it.
Good question. One moment.
You don't multiply weight by the angle. You use the cosine of the angle to find the part of the weight that pushes into the incline.
So 49 times cos 30? That's about 42.4. Then friction is 0.2 times 42.4, so 8.5?
Let me see.
Yes, that's right—multiply the weight by cos 30 to get the normal force, then multiply by the coefficient to find friction.
Okay, friction is 8.5 newtons then. Thanks.
Got it. Give me a second.
You're on the right track with the formula, but the normal force isn't 49 N on an incline. Try breaking the weight into components.
